The rebels then waited for a new caliph who, they hoped, would remove the social causes that had produced this first social revolution in Islam.

Here we should add that ʿUthmān’s social background, which we discussed earlier, was in our view a major factor in his refusal to leave office.

It was also a major factor in the style of rule that created the causes of the uprising.

One sign of this was the material luxury of his private life.

It was even said that when his daughter married, he gave her 600,000 dirhams from the state treasury, all of it drawn from jizya and kharāj—that is, for the most part, from the labor of working people.

... A number of the political groups opposed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—including ʿĀʾisha bint Abī Bakr, Ṭalḥa, and al-Zubayr—had helped stir up opposition that led to the killing of Caliph ʿUthmān.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Their anger came partly from the fact that ʿUthmān had favored the Umayyads over them in appointments to the highest offices.

At the same time, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib had sent his two sons, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, to ʿUthmān’s house to defend him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿAlī understood what ʿUthmān’s death could mean for Islam. He knew that people driven by political interests and ambition could use such an event to provoke further conflict.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Yet despite all of this, the same people who had helped encourage the movement against ʿUthmān suddenly changed their position immediately after his death.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They began demanding revenge for his blood.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They even accused ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib himself of encouraging his killing.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They did this because they feared that their own leadership and interests might face an even greater danger under ʿAlī than they had under ʿUthmān and the Umayyads.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They used ʿĀʾisha’s special position among Muslims as the Prophet’s wife and the daughter of the first caliph, Abū Bakr.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They also made use of the old resentment she held toward ʿAlī and turned it against him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They accused him of responsibility for killing the caliph in order to stir the emotions of Muslims, many of whom saw ʿUthmān’s death as a terrible and dangerous event.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿĀʾisha had personal reasons of her own for responding quickly to these pressures.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
She carried ʿUthmān’s bloodstained shirt and used it to stir public anger.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
With the support of ʿAlī’s other opponents, she was eventually able to launch the conflict known as the Battle of the Camel in Basra.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
She rode at the head of the fighters on a camel, displaying ʿUthmān’s shirt.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Battle of the Camel became the “fuse” that reignited all the political and social conflicts that had begun with Muḥammad’s death.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Although ʿAlī’s side won the battle, the fuse continued to burn and set off further explosions.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This time, however, the conflict moved onto another level: Who would become caliph after ʿUthmān?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Objectively, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was the only obvious candidate for the position at that moment.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
From the beginning of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, his name had repeatedly appeared among the candidates, only for someone else to be chosen.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
By the time ʿUthmān was killed, none of those earlier candidates remained except ʿAlī.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In the eyes of most Muslims, it therefore seemed natural that the office should now pass to him without serious competition.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But two things changed the situation in ways that few people had initially expected.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The first was the continuing effect of the Battle of the Camel.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The second was the presence in Syria of a powerful Umayyad governor who represented Umayyad leadership, aristocratic interests, and political ambition.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
That governor was Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Muʿāwiya was already governor of Syria when the uprising against ʿUthmān took place.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He had held the position since the reign of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
During his long period in power there, he built strong relations with the wealthy and influential groups of Syrian society by generally protecting their class interests.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He left the courts and police in the hands of large local landowners, wealthy townspeople, and major merchants from the local population.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He also kept customs barriers at Syria’s borders even though the country had now become part of the Arab empire.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At the same time, he imposed high customs duties on goods that competed with Syria’s more developed local products.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Muʿāwiya also exempted religious clergy of every faith from taxation.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Through this policy, he helped the dominant groups in Syria preserve full freedom to exploit the majority of the population.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In return, he secured their strong support.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He also won the sympathy of the religious leadership toward his rule.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Throughout ʿUthmān’s reign, Muʿāwiya had effectively become the absolute ruler of Syria.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He used this almost independent—or in practice fully independent—position to build another base of power that could guarantee his survival in this important office: a military base.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He created a strong army in Syria.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It was clearly Muʿāwiya’s own army rather than simply one unit within the army of the state as a whole.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

We do not know whether Muʿāwiya followed this policy simply to guarantee that he would remain governor of Syria under whichever caliph happened to rule, or whether he had already begun preparing to declare himself caliph of the Muslims when the right moment came.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But his earlier intentions are not the most important question.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

What matters is that the broad policy he had followed in Syria before the latest explosion gave him, when the “right moment” arrived, a real and material basis for declaring himself a candidate for the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He could now challenge the man whom most Muslims saw as the leading candidate for that office: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The “right moment” itself gave Muʿāwiya another advantage.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
By this we mean the fuse first lit by the Battle of the Camel against ʿAlī.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
A section of the Muslim population in Medina, Basra, and Kufa had pledged allegiance to ʿAlī as caliph.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿAlī then removed Muʿāwiya from the governorship of Syria.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In doing so, he did not fully take account of all the conditions through which Muʿāwiya had so skillfully strengthened his position.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Muʿāwiya now saw in ʿAlī’s decision a reason to aim beyond the governorship of Syria.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
All the favorable conditions had come together for him to pursue the caliphate itself.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This ambition was not simply personal.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It also expressed the ambitions of what we may call the old Umayyad aristocratic class.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This class had not been created from nothing under ʿUthmān.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Rather, during his reign it developed from a tribal aristocracy inherited from the pre-Islamic period into a class aristocracy with an increasingly semi-feudal character.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In Syria, it also became a political support and official instrument for the dominant local exploiting classes.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
There is one more factor to add: the personal qualities of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib himself.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
On one side, he came from the Hāshimite branch of Quraysh, historically opposed to the Umayyads both before and after Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
On the other, throughout the Muslim community he had a reputation for an uncompromising moral idealism.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He held firmly to ideas of truth, justice, and goodness in an absolute way and refused to compromise with those he believed had departed from them.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Once we add these features of ʿAlī to everything already described, we can understand Muʿāwiya’s position from several angles.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We can also understand the position of the class—or classes—and social groups that supported Muʿāwiya in his struggle with ʿAlī over the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It was under all these conditions that the Battle of Ṣiffīn broke out between the army of Iraq, led by ʿAlī, and the army of Syria, led by Muʿāwiya.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The fuse first lit by the Battle of the Camel was still burning.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It now set off the Battle of Ṣiffīn in 657, one year after the killing of ʿUthmān—or, in our terms, one year after the social revolution against his rule.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Khārijites emerged from the Battle of Ṣiffīn.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
With them appeared a new Islamic school, and at the same time a new political party.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Behind the religious form of their doctrine and the political form of their party lay a social ideology with democratic content.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This stood against the aristocratic—or, if the term is appropriate, class-based—content of the caliphate as it had existed before the Khārijites appeared.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We will not spend much time here on the historical details of Ṣiffīn and the events that produced the movement later known as the Khārijites.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They received this name because their founders “went out”—that is, rebelled—against the authority of the man under whose banner they had been fighting, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This happened after ʿAlī accepted a proposal from Muʿāwiya’s commanders that the Qurʾān itself be used as the judge between the two sides.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The arbitration ended in the well-known deception arranged by ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, which left ʿAlī at a disadvantage.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The irony is that the people who became the Khārijites had themselves strongly pressured ʿAlī to accept arbitration.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Yet when the arbitration ended badly for him, they turned against him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They rejected both ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya and declared both men unbelievers.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They then developed a set of principles that became the basis of a political, intellectual, and military program.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Under the banner of an Islamic religious doctrine, they pursued this program through a series of fierce and bloody conflicts.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
As an armed human group that used violence against its opponents, they eventually came to an end.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But their principles did not disappear.
